messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Car Similarity: Similar cars, Crowding: Crowded places
  Maladaptive Strategies: Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Face Hiding: cover face with hands

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus was thirty-three when he came to his first session, though the officer who had arrested him two years earlier might not have recognized him. The man who sat across from the therapist's desk was thinner, his face marked by a permanent tension around the eyes, his posture folded inward as though he were trying to take up less space. He worked as a graphic designer for a mid-sized advertising firm in Portland, a job that had once felt like a natural fit for someone who thought in images and colour. Now it felt like a cage built specifically for him.

The arrest itself had been a routine traffic stop that became something else entirely. Marcus had been driving home from a client dinner on a Friday night in March, two years prior, when he saw the lights bloom red and blue in his rearview mirror. He pulled over on a dark residential street. The officer approached his window with his hand on his holster—a gesture Marcus would later replay thousands of times—and asked for license and registration. Marcus, nervous as anyone might be, fumbled with the glove compartment. The officer, misreading the motion or perhaps simply on edge himself, yanked open the door, pulled Marcus out with force, and threw him against the car. What followed was a blur of shouting, a search that turned up nothing, and an arrest on suspicion of a crime that had occurred in a different part of the city, committed by someone who bore only a passing resemblance to Marcus. The charges were dropped within forty-eight hours. The apology came via a form letter. The memory never left.

In the months after, Marcus had noticed changes. He began drinking more—a glass of wine at dinner became two, then three, then a habit of opening a bottle alone at night to quiet the feeling of his heart accelerating in the dark. He started taking sleep medication, then anxiety medication, then something stronger that a friend had offered him. The substances helped, or seemed to, in the moment. They pushed the edge of panic back far enough that he could breathe. But they also made him unreliable. He missed deadlines at work. A client complained about the quality of his recent designs—they had become flat, lifeless, as though drawn by someone operating at half capacity. His ex-wife, whom he still saw occasionally, had asked him directly if he was using again, the word "again" carrying the weight of history neither of them wanted to revisit.

The triggers were specific and relentless. Nighttime had become something he endured rather than experienced. When he woke in the dark—and he woke often, his sleep fractured and thin—his body would flood with adrenaline, his mind convinced that he was back in that moment, that something terrible was about to happen. He had begun sleeping with the television on, the light from the screen a thin barrier against the dark. Crowded places had become intolerable. When he was forced to attend a networking event for work, the press of bodies around him, the inability to see clearly in all directions, triggered the same sensation of being trapped, of having no control over what might happen next. Worst of all were cars like the one the officer had been driving—a dark sedan, common enough that he saw them constantly. Each one made his chest tighten.

He had developed a habit of covering his face with his hands when overwhelmed, a gesture that began as a way to hide and had become almost compulsive. His colleagues had noticed. One had asked if he was okay, if something was wrong at home. He had no good answer. The uniform itself—police uniforms, security guards, even military clothing worn casually—could send him spiraling. He had started avoiding certain routes to work, certain neighborhoods, certain times of day. The world had become a landscape of threats he was learning to navigate by elimination, cutting away pieces of his life until he occupied a smaller and smaller space.

What brought him in now was a conversation with his therapist from years before—someone he had seen after his divorce—who had suggested, gently but firmly, that what he was describing sounded like something that needed proper attention. Marcus was afraid of where this was heading, afraid that naming it would make it more real. But he was also tired of drinking himself to sleep. He was tired of the constant vigilance, the exhaustion of never quite feeling safe. He wanted his life back, though he wasn't sure what that meant anymore.
